description: Hey, we’re the BBS AI Ambassador Club, a cracked crew of five middle-school students from Bayan Bilingual School, ready to take on any challenge! We’re bringing big ideas, teamwork and AI-powered creativity to build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer. Mission control, meet your next generation of space explorers!
summary:
Earth goes quiet. Six astronauts are counting on you. Can you keep a Mars outpost alive?

We are middle school students from the BBS AI Ambassadors Club in Kuwait, and our game, DEAD RECKONING: BLACKOUT, turns space science into decisions that matter. Designed for ages 7–12, it challenges players to manage air, water and power, prepare for dust and radiation hazards, and act when advice from Earth cannot arrive in time.

Our central idea is “one mission, two futures.” Players predict what will happen, try a plan, then change one preparation and replay the mission to compare the consequences. Mistakes become opportunities to investigate, explain and improve.

NASA Mars elevation data and NASA/JPL communication-delay calculations help connect the adventure to real science, while simplified game rules keep it approachable.

We collaborated on the concept, learning goals and visual direction, shared ideas and guided revisions together. With teacher guidance and AI-assisted coding and artwork, we turned our collective vision into a playable experience.

For the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge, we wanted younger learners to experience the curiosity, teamwork and problem-solving behind space exploration. Our message is simple: you do not have to be an astronaut to start thinking like one.
details:
Earth goes quiet. Six crew members are depending on you. Can your decisions keep a Mars outpost alive?

DEAD RECKONING: BLACKOUT is a browser-based space survival and learning game created by the BBS AI Ambassadors Club in Kuwait. Our team—Taher, Fahad, Mohamad and Ahmad, with our teacher mentor David—wanted to turn space science into an experience where players explore, make difficult choices and discover why their decisions matter.

Designed for young learners aged 7–12, the game puts players in charge of six crew members during a nine-day training mission. They manage connected systems such as air, water and power while preparing for dust, maintaining equipment and working with limited supplies. Communication with Earth is delayed, so players must think ahead and take responsibility for their outpost. Each day advances when the player is ready, giving them time to read, investigate and plan.

Our central idea is “One mission. Two futures.” Players predict which preparation will work best, complete their mission, and then compare it with an alternative where one preparation changes. The starting colony and outside events remain the same, making the consequences easier to understand. Would storing energy in a battery help more than improving solar generation? Players investigate the difference, explain what happened and apply their reasoning to a new situation. A setback becomes evidence for their next attempt.

Exploration makes the science tangible. Players can walk across the Martian surface and compare simulated radiation readings in open ground, near rocks and inside shelter. They can also inspect the outpost’s systems to understand what each one needs, what it produces and why it might stop working. An alternative map route makes the investigation available without first-person movement.

NASA science helps shape these experiences. NASA MOLA elevation data inform the Martian terrain, while a NASA/JPL Horizons Earth–Mars light-time record provides a reference for communication delay. We clearly distinguish these scientific inputs from our simplified teaching rules: resource production, event timing and radiation indices are game models, not real-world predictions.

We developed the game using HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Three.js for browser-based 3D graphics, Blender for original models, and Python and Node.js for supporting tools. Playwright and simulation tests helped check gameplay and technical behavior, and Vercel hosts the public game. AI tools, including Claude, OpenAI Codex and image-generation tools, supported implementation, artwork, testing and documentation under our team’s direction.

Our collaboration brought together student ideas, teacher guidance and repeated revision. We chose the concept, audience, visual direction and learning goals, then guided improvements together. We considered readability, keyboard controls, captions, sound settings, recovery after mistakes and the balance between scientific accuracy and approachable gameplay.

Our intended impact is to help children practise planning, observation and evidence-based reasoning while becoming curious about space exploration. Classroom testing is still needed to measure learning outcomes, but our goal is clear: give young players the chance to think like explorers—and discover that a better question can lead to a better mission.
